title: AD CLICK AGGREGATOR
subtitle: Clicks are money, so the numbers must be fast for dashboards and exact for billing.
footer: DDIA: Ch 11 windows, exactly-once · Ch 12 Lambda · Ch 3 column stores   ·   Similar: Top-K videos · Web crawler · Metrics monitoring · Fitness tracking

items: Redirect immediately and publish the click to Kafka; never aggregate raw rows at query time.
A stream processor counts clicks per ad per minute and writes them to a column store for fast queries.
Deduplicate by a signed impression ID, and recount from raw logs in a nightly batch job for billing accuracy.
Click on an ad redirects the user to the advertiser
Advertisers query click metrics over time (minute granularity), with filters
10k clicks/s peak, 100M/day
Never lose or double-count clicks (it is billing)
Metrics queries < 1s
Freshness ~1 minute
100M clicks × 100B ≈ 10GB/day raw.
Aggregated rows: ads × minutes, which is small.
A 10k/s peak is easy for Kafka.

blocks.text:
GET /click?ad_id&impression_id → 302 advertiser_url
GET /metrics?ad_id&from&to&granularity
click(impression_id, ad_id, ts, user) → agg(ad_id, minute, count)
Naive: insert each click into Postgres and GROUP BY at query time. Slow queries, and writes compete with reads.

items: Click service redirects immediately and publishes to Kafka. Flink aggregates per (ad, minute) on event time and upserts into an OLAP column store.
Idempotency: every impression gets a signed unique ID when the ad is served; Flink dedupes on it, so double-clicks and retries count once and forged clicks are rejected.
Lambda-style safety net: raw clicks to S3; a nightly batch recount corrects aggregates, because billing must be exact.
Flink crashes?
Checkpoints + Kafka offsets give replay; the sink upserts (ad_id, minute), so replays overwrite instead of double-counting.
Hot ad (Super Bowl)?
Key on ad_id:random(0..N) to spread across partitions, then aggregate twice.
Why also batch?
Streams give fast numbers; batch from immutable raw data gives exact billing numbers.
Why OLAP?
Column store and pre-aggregates make time-range queries over billions of rows sub-second.
Aggregating raw rows at query time in the OLTP database.
Adding parts before a number shows they are needed.
Ignoring retries, timeouts and crashes.
